en: The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī for Protecting All Children,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment, a Great Brahmā King came to visit the Buddha.
Having prostrated at the Buddha's feet, he spoke these words: "Namo Buddhāya! Namo Dharmāya!"
Namo saṃghāya. I pay homage to the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
the Great Dharma King who illuminates the world,
who first proclaimed the divine mantra and the pure, supreme Dharma of ambrosia here in Jambudvīpa.
And having paid homage to the Saṅgha of those free from attachment,
he then prostrated at the feet of the Muni and immediately spoke these verses: "O World-Honored One, among all the Tathāgatas,
Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the various sages and world-protecting kings..."
The Greatly Powerful Dragon Deity and all such multitudes were born among human beings;
there are yakṣas and rākṣasas who constantly delight in devouring human fetuses, within the realm of the non-human kings.
Unrestrained by powerful forces, it causes people to be childless and brings harm to the womb; during the union of man and woman,
it confuses their minds so that conception is not achieved.
Or Karāṇḍu and Ambu— those who cause injury to the unborn,
harm the fetus, or snatch away life at the time of birth—
all such malevolent spirits who inflict affliction upon them; I shall now speak their names.

May the Buddha grant me leave to speak of these fifteen spirits: the first is named Mīcuka; the second, King Miga; the third, Khanda; the fourth, Apasimāra; the fifth, Mocika; the sixth, Macika; the seventh, Yamika; the eighth, Kaminī; the ninth, Revati; the tenth, Pūtanā; the eleventh, Mandanandi; the twelfth, Śakunī; the thirteenth, Khaṇḍapāṇinī; the fourteenth, Mukhamanda; and the fifteenth, Lambā. These are the fifteen spirits.
Constantly wandering through the world,
he strikes fear into infants and small children.
I shall now describe the terrifying forms of these various spirits and ghosts;
by means of these forms,
I shall cause all children to give rise to fear and dread.
Miśraka is shaped like an ox; King Mṛga is shaped like a lion;
and Khaṇḍa is shaped like the god Kumāra.
The Apasmāra is shaped like a wild fox; the Mukhaka is shaped like a monkey;
and the Macchika is shaped like a rākṣasī.
Yamika has the form of a horse;
Kāminī has the form of a woman; Rēvatī has the form of a dog.
Pūtana is shaped like a pig;
Māndhātṛ is shaped like a cat; Śakuni is shaped like a bird.
Krandāvanī has a form like that of a pheasant;
Mukhamanda has a form like that of a fox;
Lambā has a form like that of a snake.
These fifteen ghosts and spirits possess small children, causing them to tremble with fear.
I shall now further describe the signs of fear that afflict these small children.
The Mīcuka spirit causes the eyes of a child to roll;
the Mīgā-rāja spirit causes a child to vomit repeatedly;
the Khaṇḍa spirit causes both shoulders of a child to twitch.
The *āpasimara* spirit enters the mouth of a small child, causing froth to emerge.
The *mucika* spirit enters a small child, causing the hands to curl so they cannot be extended.
The *macika* spirit enters a small child, causing them to bite their own tongue.
The Yāmika spirit possesses small children, causing them to weep and laugh with delight.
The Kāminī spirit possesses small children, making them take pleasure in women.
The Lepamati spirit possesses small children, causing them to perceive various diverse appearances.
The Pūtana demon possesses small children while they are asleep, causing them to cry out in terror;
the Māndākinī demon possesses small children, making them prone to weeping and laughing;
the Śakuni demon possesses small children, making them refuse to nurse.
The *khaṇḍapāṇini* ghost afflicts small children by obstructing their voices in the throat;
the *mukhamanda* ghost afflicts small children with seasonal fevers, heat illnesses, and diarrhea.
The spirit Lambā possesses small children and causes them to belch and hiccough repeatedly.
These fifteen spirits manifest in such forms as these.
I have already explained the terrors for small children, as well as the signs of their being startled and terrified.
Furthermore, there is a great king of ghost-spirits named Candana Gandharva, who is the foremost among all the ghosts and spirits.
One should [use] five-colored threads.
Recite this dhāraṇī once for each knot,
making one hundred and eight knots in total,
and write down the names of the ghosts and spirits.
He sent a messenger with this letter and spoke to that messenger, saying:
"Go now with great haste, as swift as the wind, to the four quarters."
Wherever those fifteen spirits and ghosts reside,
command the Gandharva Mahāyakṣa King Candana to bind those spirits with five-colored thread so that they shall not harass sentient beings.
Furthermore, he made offerings to the king of spirits with various delicious foods and drinks, incense, flowers, and lamps, as well as milk porridge.
At that time,
The Great Brahmā King again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there is a woman who does not give birth to sons or daughters..."
Some perish and fall away while still in the womb;
others have their lives taken after birth.
For those women who desire to obtain offspring and preserve their own long life, [they should...]
One should always maintain mindfulness and practice wholesome dharmas.
On the eighth and fifteenth days of the month, one should observe the eight precepts,
bathe until pure, and put on fresh, clean clothing.
One should pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions until midnight.
Then, taking a small amount of mustard seeds and placing them upon one's crown,
one should recite the dhāraṇī mantra as I have taught it.
May this woman immediately have her wish fulfilled;
may the son she bears be secure and free from affliction,
and throughout his entire life, may he never meet an untimely death.
"If there be any ghosts or spirits who do not obey my spell,
I shall cause their heads to split into seven pieces like the branches of an *ari* tree.
He then spoke the *dhāraṇī* spell for protecting all children.
Tadyathā: agara gani naga gani bauli jili gabali bali buli rakṣaṇe śurabhi carabhi sani paraha sani nayi minayi svāhā. World-Honored One, I now recite this dhāraṇī mantra to protect all children.
In order that they may attain peace and security and obtain long life,
at that time the World-Honored One, the Omniscient One,
spoke this incantation:

Tadyathā: Buddha buddha, buddhanumate, bodhi bodhi, malle, śikṣaya, vaśire, vatane, vārata, dhure, dhure, varadadhure, śamane, śule, vahani, dhabani, svāhā, nibarane, svāhā. These fifteen spirits constantly consume blood and flesh.
By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra,
they shall all remain far removed from it and not give rise to evil thoughts;
it shall cause these youths to be free from fear, secure, and without affliction.
When dwelling in the womb and at the time of birth, there shall be no hardships or calamities.
For those who recite this mantra,
whether in a city, a town, or a village, wherever they may dwell—
It can also cause those infants and young children to grow up in peace and security, preserving their full lifespan.
Homage to the Buddha who has accomplished this mantra.
May all children be protected from being harassed or harmed by malevolent spirits and ghosts;
may they be entirely freed from all calamities and all terrors. Svāhā!
At that time, this Brahmā Deva, having heard the exposition of this sutra, joyfully accepted and practiced it.
Thus concludes the *Buddha-spoken Sutra on the Dhāraṇī for Protecting All Children*.
